home.title: Jube Vue scaffolding
home.intro: Each card below exercises one part of the stack under Vue Vapor. Phase 0 is complete when every card reports that it works.
home.vaporBody: This page is a Vapor component rendered inside a Vapor app, with the router view interoperating through the Vapor interop plugin.
home.piniaBody: Theme preference held in the UI store: {theme}.
home.queryBody: The API and cache page drives vue-query through the single useApi function.
home.iconsBody: Lucide icons render as Vapor-compatible components.

template.label: Template
template.hint: Lay the rows out in your own markup. Print a value with a token such as [{'@'} rows[0].column {'@'}], repeat an element with v-for="row in rows", choose with v-if and v-else, put a token inside an attribute such as class="badge [{'@'} row.status {'@'}]", and format values with the number, percent, currency, date, dateTime, round, truncate, upper, lower, default and join filters, written after a pipe symbol. Names are not case sensitive. Only safe tags are allowed and every value is escaped. Use row['column name'] for names with spaces.

help.summary:
The case at a glance: what it is, why it was raised and what is at stake.
The lede at the top is built from the case's own data: the key, the workflow, the status, how old it is, and how many activations and notes it has. The fields beneath are the ones the workflow chose to display. Nothing here changes the case, so it is a safe place to start reading.
help.activations:
Every rule that fired for this case key, and why.
Each card names the rule, when it fired and how many times, so you can tell a one-off from a pattern. Counts include forced activations, which are shown as such. Use it to decide which rules to read about first before looking at the transactions themselves.
help.journal:
Every transaction on this case key, in one place, so you can read the story in order.
The lens tabs show the same transactions as payload, rules, features, models and sanctions. The strip and the charts summarise the key's own history, the Stands out list shows transactions that are unusual for this key, and the peers card shows how the key compares with other keys. Select a transaction to open its full detail, and pin it to keep it on this case.
help.network:
The entities and links around this key, such as shared devices and addresses.
This section is planned and not yet built. Until then, use Pivot and Merge in the journal to follow a shared identifier.
help.notes:
The notes written on this key, newest first, including notes from other cases on the same key.
Add a note from the Decide column. Notes are part of the audit trail and cannot be edited afterwards, so write them as you would for a reviewer who has never seen the case.
help.events:
Everything that happened to this case and key, in time order.
It joins the case's own history, such as taking, moving and closing, with earlier cases on the same key, so you can see whether it has been reviewed before and what was decided.
help.forms:
Structured forms for this workflow, such as a suspicious activity report.
Every form submitted on this case key is drawn here read only, newest first, from the form's current layout. Values the layout no longer has a field for are listed beneath it. Open a form from the Decide column to fill one in.
help.messages:
Everything the case workflow sent for this case key, newest first: emails, texts and web calls fired by a form, a macro, an action or a status.
Each one shows whether it was sent, failed or was refused before it left, where it went, what it said, and how it was drawn (from the stored payload or from the record's SQL, with the rows it used). Open the message or the rows to read exactly what was sent.

decide.title:
Everything you can do to this case.
Taking a case locks it to you, so nobody else can change it. A supervisor can break the lock. Release the case if you stop working on it so it returns to the queue. Close and reopen sit lower down.

help.dashboard: A dashboard built for this kind of case by whoever configured the workflow. It can describe the whole case, not only its transactions, and it is drawn from the case key and its value alone: anything else it shows is worked out from those two.

hold.title: Held payment

hold.none: No payment is held, declined, released or refused on this case.
hold.failed: The held payments could not be loaded.

charts.drift: Drift between earlier and recent history

help.field:
Chooses which numeric field the first two charts draw.
The list holds the fields the journal treats as measures for this key: payload fields your roles may see, plus features and model scores.
It does not change the other charts, which look at all of the key's transactions.
help.progression:
Shows how the chosen field has moved over time for this key.
Each point is the median of the transactions in one hour, one day or one week, whichever fits the history: hours when it spans three days or less, days up to about seven months, weeks beyond that. A median is used so that one unusual transaction does not drag the line.
Look for steps, ramps and gaps. A step means behaviour changed on a date, a ramp means something is building, and a point far from its neighbours is worth finding in the grid. The subtitle gives the latest value.
It is empty when no transaction in the window has this field.
help.distribution:
Shows how the chosen field is spread across this key's transactions.
Each bar counts the transactions whose value falls in a range, with between 5 and 40 ranges chosen from the data. The subtitle says where the latest value sits as a percentile of the key's own history: the 99th percentile means it is larger than 99 percent of what this key has done.
A long tail to the right means a few large transactions. Two humps mean two kinds of behaviour.
This compares the key with itself. Compared with peers, above the grid, compares it with other keys.
It is empty when no transaction has this field.
help.velocity:
Shows when this key's transactions happen, by day of the week and hour of the day.
Each cell is a count and the darker the cell the more transactions. Rows are weekdays and columns are hours. The hours are UTC, not the customer's local time.
A key that suddenly moves money at 03:00 on a Sunday, when it normally trades on weekday afternoons, shows one dark cell in a pale area.
It is empty when the window has no transactions.
help.gaps:
Shows how long the key was quiet before each transaction.
Each bar counts transactions by the time since the previous one, from minutes to weeks. Tall bars on the left mean bursts, and bars on the far right mean long dormancy before activity.
A burst after a long quiet period is a classic sign of an account being taken over or used to pass money through.
The first transaction has no gap, so it is empty when the key has fewer than two transactions in the window.
help.correlation:
Shows which numeric fields rise and fall together for this key.
Each cell is a Pearson correlation coefficient, r, between two fields: 1 means they move in step, -1 means they move in opposite directions and 0 means no relationship. Only fields with at least 10 transactions that have both values are compared, and the chart appears only when at least one pair has r of 0.8 or more, in either direction.
An amount and the balance after it will usually correlate. A new strong link between fields that were unrelated before is more interesting than an old one. Correlation does not show cause.
It is empty when no pair is strong enough, which is normal, and always for a key with fewer than 10 transactions.
help.drift:
Shows whether a field behaves differently in the key's recent history than in its earlier history.
The window is split in two, earlier and recent. For each field the first bar is the distance between the two distributions (the Kolmogorov distance) and the second bar is the critical value. A field whose distance is above the critical value has drifted at the 5 percent significance level.
Drift means the key's normal has moved, so comparisons with its older history may no longer apply. A key that has drifted is often one whose purpose or controller has changed.
It needs at least 40 transactions with at least 20 on each side, so it is empty below that, and also when no field has drifted.
help.counterparties:
Shows who this key deals with most often.
Each bar is a counterparty, the other party to a transaction, ranked by how many transactions the key had with it. The subtitle says how many different counterparties there were and how many appeared for the first time in the last 30 days.
A key spread over many one-off counterparties looks different from one concentrated on a few regular ones, and a sudden rush of new counterparties is a pattern worth a look.
Only fields the workflow marks as a counterparty are charted. It is empty when none are marked or the key has none.

help.lens:
Shows the same transactions through different sets of columns, so you can read one transaction from several angles.
Payload is the transaction's own fields that your roles may see. Rules shows which activations fired, and which of them were forced. Features shows what the rules saw: counters, calculations and dictionaries. Models shows Exhaustive and Advanced Analytics scores. Sanctions shows sanction distances and HTTP adaptations.
The number on each tab is how many transactions have something to show in that lens. A lens with 0 has nothing for this key and window.
help.activationsOnly:
Shows only the transactions that raised at least one activation.
Use it to get from a long history to the moments the rules reacted. It also narrows the charts, the statistics and Tag all matching to those transactions.
help.pinnedOnly:
Shows only the transactions pinned on this case, whatever their date or key.
Pins are for the whole case, so everyone working it sees the same ones. Pin a transaction with the star in the grid. Pinned transactions are also always at the top of the journal, in every lens, even outside the window.
A case can hold up to 50 pins, and a case locked to another user cannot be changed.
help.tags:
Tags label transactions, for example mule or reviewed, so they can be found and counted later.
Tick rows in the grid, then press Tag to add or remove tags on all of them at once, up to 500. Undo appears afterwards. Transactions whose case is locked to another user are left alone and counted.
Tag all matching tags every transaction of the current view, up to 100,000, in the background. You can keep working, stop it, and undo it afterwards. Only tags set up for this workflow's model can be added.
help.transactions:
How many transactions this key had in the window, newest first, up to 2,000.
The strip, the stands-out list and the charts are all worked out from these transactions. When the key has more, the strip says so and the older ones are left out of the statistics but not of the grid.
help.activeDays:
The number of different days, in UTC, on which the key had at least one transaction.
Read it with the transaction count: many transactions on few days means activity in bursts, and few transactions spread over many days means steady, slow use.
help.withActivations:
How many of the transactions raised at least one activation, and how many activations were raised in total.
One transaction can raise several activations, so the second figure can be larger than the first.
help.elevation:
The highest response elevation of any transaction in the window.
Elevation is the weight the rules gave a transaction when it fired: the higher it is, the more urgent the response.
help.field:
The latest value of this numeric field for the key, and its typical value, which is the median over the window.
A Stands out badge appears when the latest transactions are far from this key's own normal for the field. The first three measures of the key are shown.
help.notable:
Transactions that stand out against this key's own history.
Each numeric field of a transaction is scored by how far it is from the key's median, in units of the key's usual spread. The spread is the median absolute deviation, so that unusual values do not hide themselves by inflating it. A score of 3 or more is listed, with the field that stands out most named, up to 5 rows.
A field with fewer than 5 values is not judged, and under 20 transactions the statistics are marked low confidence. Select a row to open the transaction.
help.peers:
How this key compares with the other keys of the same workflow and case key, field by field.
Each figure is this key's median against the spread of every key's median, built by the jobs server from recent history and refreshed daily by default. The bar is the percentile among peers, and a field is called above or below peers when it is 3 or more spreads from the peers' median.
If the workflow has a segment field, such as customer tier, the comparison is with keys in the same segment, falling back to all keys when the segment has none. It reads not built until the jobs server has built the distributions.

drawer.activations:
The activations that fired on this transaction.
A forced activation was triggered because someone forced the rule through, rather than because the transaction met its condition. Only activations your roles may see are listed.
drawer.models:
What each scoring model made of this transaction, as it was when it scored.
For each model: the score, the threshold, whether it crossed it, the calibrated probability, the contribution of each input, and the decision path the model followed. The contribution is drawn as a waterfall when it adds up exactly, and otherwise as signed bars that do not add up.
Inputs your roles may not see are hidden, with only a count shown.
drawer.values:
What the rules saw when this transaction was processed.
Counters, calculations, dictionaries, sanction distances and HTTP adaptation values, grouped by where they come from. They are frozen as they were then, so they can differ from what the same counter says now.
drawer.keys:
The identifiers on this transaction, such as account, device and address.
Pivot shows the whole journal for that value instead of the case key, with a way back. Merge adds it as a lane next to the case key so the two share one timeline. Only identifiers marked as drill fields on the workflow can be used.
drawer.around:
Shows what else happened on the same day (UTC) that shared an identifier with this transaction.
Each group is one identifier of the transaction, with the other transactions that used it that day, newest first, up to 25. Open a row to move to that transaction.
It helps to see whether a device or address was busy elsewhere at the same time.
drawer.payload:
The raw fields of the transaction as it arrived, limited to the ones your roles may see.
It is not loaded until you ask, because reading it is recorded in the audit trail: who looked at the raw transaction and when.
drawer.highlights:
Why this transaction is coloured in the grid.
Your administrator sets the colours for a workflow. A bold row is a transaction that has the same value as the case itself for a field chosen to be matched, such as the same device or account, so it stands out among the others on the key. A coloured cell or row is a field whose value matches the pattern configured for it.
Colour is never the only signal: every reason is written out here and in the Highlighted because column of the grid.

help.columns:
Chooses which columns the grid shows.
Drag a column heading to move it and drag its edge to resize it. Switch a column off to hide it, and the switch brings it back. The Select, Actions and Pin columns stay put.
Your arrangement is saved for you and for this lens, and is there next time you open any case in this workflow. Reset layout returns the lens to its default columns.
help.filter:
Narrows the transactions to those that match conditions you build on the Archive.
Each condition is a field of the model (payload, abstractions, counters and so on), an operator and a value, for example Payload.Amount greater than 1000. Combine conditions with and or or, and add groups for more complicated questions. Like and not like use the percent sign as a wildcard.
The filter applies in the Archive before the row limit, so it finds matching transactions even when they would not all fit in the grid, and it appears in the address so you can share it. The count shows how many of the key's transactions in the window match. The statistics, charts, peers and lens counts deliberately keep using the whole window, so filtering down to unusual transactions cannot make them look normal.
Tag all matching tags every transaction the filter leaves, up to 100,000, using the same filter, so the count in the dialog is exact.
help.format:
Colours and bold lines set by your administrator for this workflow.
A bold row shares a configured value with the case itself, for example the same device. A coloured cell, or a whole coloured row, is a value that matches the pattern configured for that field. Each one says why in the Highlighted because column, and the same reasons are in the transaction panel.
help.scope:
The keys and the filter narrow the grid and the map below. The statistics and charts above are not affected by them, so filtering down to unusual transactions cannot make them look normal.
The case key is always lane A. Extra keys are added as lanes of their own, up to three, chosen from the workflow's drill fields, for example the device an account used, and each has its own trail on the map. Conditions narrow the transactions to those that match them anywhere in the Archive, and you can combine them with and or or in the filter dialog.
Save view keeps the window, the keys, the filter and the map options so anyone on the case can open the same view again.
help.window: How far back the journal looks, from today. It applies to everything on this card and above: the statistics, the charts, the grid and the map.

help.limits:
Decide what counts as movement that could not have happened.
A leg is the journey between two consecutive transactions of a trail. It is marked impossible when it is at least the shortest leg and the speed needed to cover it in the time between the two transactions is above the speed limit. The defaults are 900 kilometres an hour, about the speed of an airliner, and 50 kilometres, so that a short hop between two nearby positions is never flagged however quickly it happened.
Lower the speed limit to look for travel that was possible only by air, and raise it to see only the extreme cases. The limits are kept in the address and saved with a replay, so the same replay counts the same legs each time.
help.only:
Draws only the movement worth a look.
With this on, the map keeps just the legs that are impossible at the speed limit and shortest leg set here, together with the transactions at either end of each, and hides every ordinary journey. Each key still has its own trail. If nothing is left, no leg breaks the limits you have set, which is itself an answer.
The setting is kept in the address and saved with a replay.
help.all:
Draws every transaction of the key, its extra keys and the window, and picks out the ones your filter matches.
The matching transactions are drawn in full colour and join up into trails. The others are drawn faint and grey, and never join a trail, so they give context without changing the movement. The counts, the legs, the impossible journeys and the worst journey below still cover only the matching transactions.
The setting is kept in the address. It only does something while a filter is set.
